Pele Yoetz 40:2: And from this you shall hear how great is the evil of the sinner, and especially the sin of the emission of seed in vain, which causes the husk to oppress holy souls, and the sparks of holiness descend anew into the depths of the husks. How much distress it causes the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, for those souls are like prisoners in a prison house, groaning the groan of the slain, and the Shechinah cries out: "would that my head were water and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people" (Jeremiah 8:23). And of them David said (Psalms 79:11): "let the groan of the prisoner come before You; according to the greatness of Your arm, spare those condemned to death," and so on. Over this a man shall tremble and be seized, and shall run to a mitzvah and flee from transgression (Avot 4:2). And he shall be very careful with the blessings over enjoyment, for through the blessings the clarification of holiness is accomplished from foods, and therefore he shall be very careful to recite them precisely - for if he is not careful, he injures a soul. And let all his deeds be for the sake of Heaven (Avot 2:12), provided he conducts his affairs with judgment according to the Torah, by measure, by weight, and by measure of capacity - and then He shall cause the horn of salvation to sprout speedily in our days, Amen, so may it be His will.
Pele Yoetz 41:1: Checking - It is our great obligation to check thoroughly for forbidden things so as not to stumble into them, and especially regarding the matter of insects the stumbling is great, for there are many kinds of fruits and vegetables in which insects are found, and many of the common people are not careful and eat them without checking. And likewise with matzah meal or flour, mostly there are thousands of tiny worms in it that are not visible to the eye, but when the flour is held up against the sun, then they can be seen moving - and there is no remedy except to first strain it through a thick cloth and then boil it over the fire and strain it again. And likewise regarding strawberries [or a similar fruit], they have testified that there are worms in them that cannot be found by checking, and a God-fearing person should treat them as entirely forbidden. And they likewise wrote that a God-fearing person should not eat raw vegetables or pickled cabbage even with checking, and all the more so without checking, which is an outright prohibition - and they have already cried out a great and bitter outcry about this in the books, for whoever calls himself by the name of Israel would not eat carrion or a torn animal or pork and the like even if given all the silver and gold in the world, and if forced, would suffer bitter punishments unto death rather than transgress, even though his palate might crave to taste the delicacies made from pig and the like - yet have you considered that in eating carrion, a torn animal, and pork there is only one prohibition, while in eating a single insect there are four prohibitions, and in eating an ant or any flying creeping thing there are five prohibitions? It is found that one who eats without care and without checking eats, within a brief moment, a hundred insects and transgresses heaps upon heaps of prohibitions with contempt of soul, without any benefit at all, merely from lack of care. Of this and the like it is said (Isaiah 5:18): "woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity." Behold, therefore, "put a knife to your throat if you are a man given to appetite" (Proverbs 23:2). And one must warn the people of this and the like, for the holy people of Israel wish to be disciplined and abstinent, but they err unwittingly - may the good LORD atone for them. And whoever warns shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who bring merit to the many shall shine like the stars (Daniel 12:3), and it shall be pleasant to those who listen, and a blessing of good shall come upon them, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 42:1: Letter Gimel: Redemption - We shall have redemption speedily in our days, Amen - so must one believe with complete faith, and this is among the principles of the faith, and it is one of the questions asked at the day of judgment: did you await salvation (Shabbat 31a, Sanhedrin 5a) (and as shall be written further under the entry "Tzafui" [awaited]). And among the signs of one who believes in and awaits salvation is that regarding every matter he speaks of for the distant future, he shall say: the Holy One, blessed be He, shall cause the horn of salvation to sprout beforehand - and likewise that he not build many strong houses and spacious upper rooms with decorations and carved ornaments in a foreign land, for whoever has a settled and confident heart sits and awaits, day by day, that the day of the LORD is near, when He shall gather in the scattered, and "let us arise and go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the place of our sanctuary," and he shall not establish a fine dwelling for himself in the impure land - all the more so since his own days are like a passing shadow and we are strangers in this world. And since the life of man in this world is vanity, and whether in blessings of good or when days of evil come, it is all the same, for man does not know what is good, and there is no good for man in his labor except when he gives peace of mind to his Maker - therefore it is not fitting to desire the redemption in order to rest and see good, but rather to serve the LORD and for the honor of the Shechinah of our strength and the honor of our Father in Heaven, for great is the distress of Heaven, to a place beyond what our own hand can reach - this is the entire fruit of our deeds and our prayer, and this applies to every person.
Pele Yoetz 43:1: Pride - Its great evil is explained in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, in the Talmud, the Midrashim, and all the holy books. And who can belittle what is written (Proverbs 16:5): "an abomination to the LORD is every proud heart"? And they said (Sotah 5a): let whoever has it be under a ban. And it is considered as though he worshiped idols and as though he had relations with all forbidden unions, and his dust shall not be stirred at the resurrection of the dead, and many other such evils. And all the world's creatures know the great evil of pride, but the trouble is that they think the essence of pride is walking with an erect posture and swinging one's arms this way and that, while we do not know what pride truly is - but there is a sign, from the strength of the son to recognize the strength of the father, for exactingness and anger and the like are the children of pride, and if there are no fathers, from where would the offspring come (as shall be written below under the entry "Toldot" [offspring])? And so greatly has the enemy, the evil inclination, prevailed, that it shows a person that exactingness, grievance, and anger are the perfection of good traits, to the point that they say: whoever does not feel [insulted] is not human.
Pele Yoetz 43:2: And the man who fears the LORD and is tender of heart - let his hair stand on end at seeing the severity and greatness of the evil of pride, and let his heart be kindled at seeing the greatness of the praise of humility, and let him strive with all his strength, with pure thoughts, to recognize his own small worth and be despised in his own eyes, loathsome, to be among those who are insulted by every person, even the members of his own household, and let him not be exacting, and not become angry, and not complain at all, but rather be exceedingly humble in spirit and humble of knee. And the great fence for this is the constant reading of books of ethics and fulfilling the verse (Psalms 51:5), "and my sin is always before me." And even if his hand has attained great wisdom and knowledge, exposition is not the main thing, and everything is according to the abundance of deeds, according to what kind of person he is - a scale and just balances are in the hand of the LORD - and let him take to heart that, according to his own measure and knowledge and understanding and preparation and the kindness his Maker bestowed upon him, he has still not discharged one part in a thousand of his obligation, and "he who increases knowledge increases pain" (Ecclesiastes 1:18) - pain over what he should have done but did not do, and where he could have attained more but did not strive to attain it, for judgment belongs to God.
Pele Yoetz 43:3: And let him judge every person favorably (Avot 1:6). And if he sees with his own eyes and clearly understands in his heart that his fellow, or his wife, or even his son and his student and his servant, has sinned against him and treated him improperly, it is fitting that he not become angry and not be distressed and not be exacting at all - for "why should a living man complain, a man for his own sins?" (Lamentations 3:39), and the LORD told him to curse. And moreover, if a person like himself makes light of his honor or treats it heavily, what does it give him and what does it add to him - all is vanity and vexation of spirit (Ecclesiastes, various verses).
Pele Yoetz 43:4: And according to the greatness of the good that comes to those who are insulted, it is found, according to truth, that his fellow has performed a great good for him, and it is fitting to rejoice more in those who disgrace him than in those who honor him - only he shall be pained that his fellow has sinned and caused distress and blemish above. Therefore let him make a fence for himself as best he can so that others not sin against him and not talk back to him, and if they do sin, let him strive to rebuke them if his words are heeded, and find ways for them to come and appease him and correct their wrongdoing and not continue to sin - all in a proper manner, so that no mishap of gossip or desecration of the Name results, God forbid. And every clever person shall act with knowledge, conducting his affairs with judgment according to what kind of person he is, the place, and the need of the hour - if reverence is needed, he shall show anger and exactingness, but his heart shall be hollow within him, and all his deeds shall be for the sake of Heaven, and the LORD shall not withhold good from those who walk in innocence. And the fence they set against coming to pride is to flee from honor, and all the more so not to seek greatness. (And included in this, I say, is that one who composes a book should not seek approbations, for this is like saying "honor me, please," which is well known - for approbations are meant to glorify and exalt the author, and what does it give if people say his name is great - what does it give and what does it add?)
Pele Yoetz 44:1: Theft - The severity of the sin of theft is known, to the point that they said (Sanhedrin 108a) that the verdict of the generation of the Flood was sealed only because of theft. And as long as one has stolen property in his hand, his prayer is not heard (Shemot Rabbah 22:3), and in the World to Come they feed him coals of broom bushes, and he must return in transmigration to make repayment. And I have already recorded, in the pamphlet "Orot Elim" (page 113), a wondrous incident that happened in the days of the master Rabbi Yisrael Ba'al Shem Tov, that a certain man came back in the transmigration of a horse and labored with all his strength in order to repay his debt. And some have written on the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Yoma 85a), that for transgressions between man and his fellow, Yom Kippur does not atone until he has appeased his fellow - meaning that even transgressions between man and the Omnipresent are not forgiven until he has returned the stolen item and appeased his fellow (and see what is written below under the entry "Teshuvah" [repentance]). And alas for those who are found among us, for whom theft has become like something permitted because they have changed its name, calling it by the name of shrewdness, diligence, and effort, and give thanks to God for what he has done and succeeded in.
Pele Yoetz 44:2: And there are several kinds of theft that many have trampled upon; we shall mention some of them - let the listener listen and the one who ceases, cease, and upon him shall come a blessing of good. First to come out is an evil and bitter custom found in the world: the man whose hand has become weak and who does not have as much property as he wishes, or who has become entirely poor - what does he do? He goes to the cities of Edom, such as Vienna, Venice, Leipzig, and the like, and takes a large amount of merchandise on credit with the intention of not paying, or takes from the people of his own city and afterward shows that he has gone bankrupt, and through bribing the judges of the land does whatever he wants, and after some time, against their will and to their disadvantage, the creditors settle for twenty percent or thirty percent [of what is owed]. And if they call a man who goes out in the middle of the road and robs passersby a robber, and by the opinion of all the world's creatures he deserves to be put to death - when we examine it carefully, one who does these things is worse than that robber in several respects. First, that a person can guard himself against a robber. And further, that the robber received no benefit from this man whom he robbed, but when a wicked man borrows with the intent not to repay, it is found that he is ungrateful and repays evil for good to the man who trusted him and did him a kindness by lending to him - and it is written (Proverbs 17:13), "whoever repays evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house." And further, the robber steals only money, while this one steals money and people's trust as well. And further, "he who locks the door against borrowers shall be struck like Rava" [i.e. suffers consequences too] (Bava Kamma 92a). And further, if they catch the robber, he shall pay in full and be flogged and pay - but not so this one, who by the power of idolatrous judges can eat and enjoy his fellow's money and do whatever his heart desires, while the creditor watches and, enraged, gnashes his teeth and melts away, with no savior except the LORD, who shall plead their cause and take the life of those who rob them (Proverbs 22:23). And I testify that I have seen many men who did this, and the verse was fulfilled in them (Jeremiah 17:11): "he who makes wealth unjustly shall leave it in the midst of his days, and in his end he shall be a base fool." And even what was in their hand was lost from them, for such is the standard - this one comes and destroys that one - besides his punishment reserved for him in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 44:3: And it is known that theft from a gentile is more severe than theft from a Jew, for the severe sin of desecration of the Name accompanies it, and the Kabbalists wrote that a Jew who robs a gentile causes the gentile's guardian angel to rob abundance from holiness for the husk. And although we hold (Choshen Mishpat 348:2) that deceiving an idolater [in matters of legally overlooked error] is permitted, it is forbidden to actively mislead him - even to sell him carrion and tell him it is properly slaughtered, or to give him counterfeit coins and tell him they are good, or to mix them with good ones and the like - all of this is forbidden and is called outright theft. And there is another kind of theft found among partners: when one is stingy about spending on his household, his partner comes and gives to his wife without his knowledge, and takes the equivalent from the partnership funds - this is theft, and he sins and it is not his to take. There is a straight path for a man to follow, and this matter is especially common among women, giving charity or gifts or making expenditures without the owner's knowledge - this too is called theft. One who borrows without permission is a thief (Bava Metzia 41a). And there is much that is similarly [taken without full consent] regarding shoes, books, and the like. How very much must one be careful and weigh in the balance not to accept and not to eat from a man who says to him, while eating and drinking, "eat and drink," while his heart is not with him [i.e., he doesn't truly mean it], or who reduces the amount out of embarrassment - for there is an element of theft in this (Sefer Chasidim 316). And there is a group of friends who take from their friends in the manner of a gift, or cheaply, against the will and to the disadvantage of the owners - this is outright theft, and moreover they transgress the prohibition of "you shall not covet."
Pele Yoetz 44:4: Craftsmen, and especially teachers of young children, if they do not do their work faithfully, their hand is in trespass and there is theft in their hands.
Pele Yoetz 44:5: It is written (Proverbs 28:24): "whoever robs his father or mother and says, 'it is no transgression,' is a companion to a destroyer." And it is because of our sins that there are many wayward children, in whom there is no faithfulness, who rob their father and mother. And whoever has not taken this to heart and has stumbled into robbing his father, and has not asked his forgiveness, shall make amends by reconciling with him.
Pele Yoetz 44:6: How very much must one be careful with theft from the public, for it is found that he multiplies transgressions equal to the number of people from whom he stole - and if even in robbing a single individual it is difficult to return the stolen and already consumed property, all the more so for one who robs the public, whose repentance is difficult - therefore one must be very careful. And those who are obligated to pay taxes and the like to the community and pay with bad coins, causing loss to the public, have theft from the public in their hands. And there are many such branches and offshoots of theft, and permissive paths that a man following the counsel of his own inclination teaches himself, one who does not come to seek God and hear teachings.
Pele Yoetz 44:7: And there is also theft that is not theft by human law but is theft by the law of Heaven - such as one who entrenches himself stubbornly on a point of halachah to litigate with his fellow in a matter of Torah law and collect money from him for no wrong done by his own hands, but rather because his own eye deceived him and caused loss to his fellow, not through rebellion or trespass but with a simple heart and clean hands, like a person doing what is rightfully his own - and even if by strict law he is liable to pay in such a case, the spirit of the Omnipresent is not at ease with him, and by doing this he withholds a kindness from his fellow and transgresses "love your fellow as yourself," which is a great principle of the Torah - and of such a case they said (Eruvin 65b): a person is recognized by his pocket. And according to the severity of the prohibition of theft and the difficulty of its repentance - for they said (Bava Kamma 119a) that whoever robs his fellow of even a perutah's worth is as though he had robbed him of his own soul and the souls of his sons and daughters, and as long as the stolen item remains in his hand he has no atonement whatsoever, and it is difficult to return stolen property that has already been consumed (Chullin 89a) - behold, therefore, the man who fears the LORD shall be careful and guard himself very much from any kind of theft in whatever manner it may occur, and his business dealings shall be in good faith. And even if the hour presses him greatly and his creditors press him with severe penalties, he shall not, because of this, stretch out his hand to theft, God forbid - for it is better for a person to die of hunger than to be wicked before the Omnipresent for even one hour, and "those who seek the LORD shall not lack any good" (Psalms 34:11), for the LORD shall not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 45:1: Stealing - It is known, the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Bava Kamma 79b), that it is more severe than robbery, for it does not equate the servant with his Master, acting as though the Eye above does not see. And how very much one must warn adults about children, for many young children steal and bad companions cause it, and they go from evil to evil, becoming gluttons and drunkards - therefore one must keep watchful eyes over them. And it is good for a man not to be so restrictive with his children, but to loosen his hand a little to give them some coins from time to time, so that they not be craving and hungry for everything and come to steal - and likewise he should not accustom them to fine foods, expensive clothing, and human pleasures, for when they can no longer obtain what they are accustomed to, they shall come to steal, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 72a) that the Torah understood the mind of the wayward and rebellious son, that when he cannot obtain what he is accustomed to, he shall rob people. And it was already told, an incident about a certain Torah scholar whose father raised him in luxury according to his wealth, and after his father's death he lost the wealth and sought his accustomed luxury, until he came to steal books from the study house, and when the matter was discovered he converted his religion, may the Merciful One save us. Therefore every clever person shall act with knowledge and conduct his affairs with judgment - not being too restrictive nor too extravagant, but rather conducting himself in a complete middle way according to the blessing the LORD has given him, and shall always warn his children about forbidden things and inform them of their severity, and keep them far from the company of evildoers, so that they walk in the way of the good.
Pele Yoetz 45:2: And there is another kind of stealing that many have trampled upon - namely, stealing people's minds [deceiving them]. And there are various kinds of this. The general principle is: whoever strives to know what is in his fellow's heart through excessive words is called stealing his mind and it is forbidden - unless he does it for the sake of Heaven, to save an oppressed person from his oppressor or to keep him from a prohibition. And likewise, one who shows excessive affection to his fellow while his mouth and his heart do not match is called stealing his mind, and "whoever walks in innocence shall walk securely."
Pele Yoetz 46:1: Might - Might is a great principle in the Torah. "Who is mighty? He who conquers his own inclination" (Avot 4:1). And happy is he who overcomes his inclination like a man, running to every mitzvah and fleeing from transgression (Avot 4:2) and from every evil trait, and fulfilling every good thing and matters of piety in all their details, repairs, and fine points, in thought, speech, and deed, with all his heart, all his soul, and all his might, and being slow to anger, which is better than might (Proverbs 16:32), and fulfilling the ways of repentance and afflicting his body, and many such things - whoever his inclination overpowers and he conquers it is called mighty. And blessed is He who gives strength to the weary, for every person has strength commensurate to what he is, and although the evil inclination is fire and makes war with schemes, renewing and strengthening itself against a person every day and every hour, every man and woman whose hearts move them to fight against it, with help from the Almighty, can overcome it - only the beginnings are difficult, and afterward it becomes easy for him and pleasant and sweet.
Pele Yoetz 46:2: And it is especially necessary to be careful and diligent - "strength shall increase" for whoever his inclination has overpowered and he has trampled upon transgressions until they have become like something permitted to him - he must strengthen himself to separate from the transgression as one separates from a grave. For example, one whose nature is evil and who is accustomed to bad traits or excessive drinking, or to habitual gambling, or to mentioning the Name of the LORD in vain, or to false oaths, or to wasting time in vanity and emptiness, and many such matters that many have trampled upon and all similar to them - he must give his very soul to separate from them, and be like a soldier standing guard, with strategies, fences, and safeguards, reckoning the reward of a mitzvah against the reward of a transgression and so on, and that reward is according to the pain, and that love for our Father in Heaven should be as fierce as death, to the point of fulfilling "for Your sake we are slain all day long" and "we have loved You unto death." And after all the labor and toil, mercy must be sought from our God - may the Merciful One have mercy and help us for the sake of the honor of His Name, forever and ever, Amen, so may it be His will.
Pele Yoetz 47:1: Exile - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avot 4:14): exile yourself to a place of Torah. And it is true that our Rabbis, of blessed memory, also said: it is a mitzvah for a person to dwell in the place of his ancestors, and like a bird wandering from its nest, so is a man who wanders from his place, and it is impossible for a person to uproot his dwelling from his established place - but if it happens that he is forced to uproot his dwelling from his place, in the manner of their saying, of blessed memory (Bava Metzia 75b), "whoever is embarrassed in this town, let him go to another town," let him choose to exile himself to a place of Torah, for he is assured that his children shall be Torah scholars, and he too shall learn the statutes and the ordinances and walk in the way of the good. And Rabbi Yose ben Kisma spoke well (Avot 6:9): even if you gave me all the silver and gold in the world, I would dwell only in a place of Torah - for if he learns one good thing, that suffices him. And included in this is that whoever wishes to merit the crown of Torah and does not find in his own place anyone from whom to learn, his father should send him, or he should go himself, to a city of sages and scholars to study Torah, and he should not worry about the trouble or the separation or the expense, for all of it is as nothing compared to the good of meriting the crown of Torah - and even if there is a sage in his own city, sometimes he can learn better when exiled to another city, as the Tosafot wrote (Shabbat 9b, s.v. "ha lan") that such was the custom of the earlier generations, that the people of the Land of Israel would go to study Torah in Babylon in order to be settled without disturbance.
Pele Yoetz 47:2: And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Eruvin 55a) on the verse (Deuteronomy 30:12), "it is not in heaven" - for if it were in heaven, you would need to go after it - "nor is it across the sea" - for if it were across the sea, you would need to go after it. If only fathers and sons understood how great is the good of one who merits that his children be sons of Torah - they would sell their clothing and send their children to a place of Torah, even to the end of the world. And the special property of Torah is that it is acquired more through exile and wandering, and therefore they said, go forth and learn. And everything depends on what kind of person he is - in these generations, if he has someone from whom to learn in his own place in a settled manner, it is better that he not move from his place, so that a father's eyes remain open over his children, and if he is married, that he remain near his wife.
Pele Yoetz 47:3: And if he must be exiled either for the sake of Torah or because he travels the roads for his livelihood, in the manner of merchants, it is good for a man to intend and pour out his own conversation that this journey be significant to him as an exile, and that he accept the decree of Heaven with love, to be exiled for the atonement of sins, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 37b): exile atones for sin - provided he guards himself on the journey he travels from every evil thing, so that he not be like one who cleanses on one side and soils on the other. And if it is not arranged for him by decree of Heaven to travel the roads, there is one who uproots his dwelling from house to house, which is also considered exile, and he should intend this - for they said (Pesikta DeRav Kahana, ch. 29) that the reason we go into exile during the festival from the house to the sukkah is for us to have an exile that atones for sin. And he should intend this likewise when going from his house to the synagogue or the study house, and it is very hard for him on a stormy day and he carries an umbrella, or when he sits all night in the study house and cannot settle in his sitting and lying as at home - let him accept it with love and do it with joy, and let him prepare himself that it be an exile that atones for sin. And likewise on the eves of Passover, when they empty the houses for the search for chametz and seat the master of the house between the oven and the stove, let him accept it with love and intend that it be an exile that atones. And so with any similar journey or displacement that he is forced to undertake, whether for a mitzvah matter or for the need of his livelihood, let him intend and seek that it be considered an exile that atones for sin - as they said (Kohelet Rabbah 7:27), "what does it matter to me whether it is a whole soul or part of a soul" - so is this matter: what does it matter to me whether the exile is great or small - it all counts to the reckoning, provided he directs his heart to this and accepts it with great love.
Pele Yoetz 47:4: And behold, it is known, the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, that exile has left no good trait for Israel. And they [others] said: exile is fitting for Israel. And I say the explanation of the matter is that exile of the soul is not good for Israel, and it is fitting for whoever has the ability to flee from a place that oppresses Israel in matters touching the soul - such as places where a man is not permitted to marry until another married man from the city has died, or places where Jews are forcibly taken and made to be soldiers, compelled to leave the status of individuals [devoted to Torah study], and many such harsh decrees and evil customs found in some kingdoms - whoever has the ability to uproot his dwelling and flee from there and does not strive to do so is destined to give an account, for it is more fitting to flee from such places than from a place where there is plague or disease, God forbid. And if they do not leave for the sake of their money, their money too is lost, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 112b): what caused the righteous to dwell among the wicked? Their money - therefore their money was lost. Learn from this that it is fitting to be exiled and flee from a city whose inhabitants are wicked if he cannot correct it and has no power to protest, lest he be swept away in the sin of the city and lest he be burned by their glowing coals.
Pele Yoetz 47:5: But regarding matters touching the body, exile is fitting for Israel, and it is not good for a man to dwell in the cities of Italy and the cities of Edom and the like, for because of the freedom there, a person cannot protest against transgressors, and there is no authority for Jewish law to judge between a man and his fellow, but rather everyone is judged by gentile courts, and a sage has no power to punish. Behold, therefore, "Yeshurun grew fat and kicked" (Deuteronomy 32:15), and the man who is upright in his own eyes and perverse does as he pleases, since there is no one to say to him what are you doing and what are you performing. And the sickest evil of all is that they are not careful about [immodest] hearing, and they are lax in matters of forbidden relations, and the gentile women go about openly and immodestly, and there are brothels of harlots - and because of this, the Jews who dwell among them mix with the gentiles and learn their deeds.
Pele Yoetz 47:6: And likewise there is a sick evil in the cities of Edom, that a grown beard is a disgrace to them, and because of this, among the Jews who dwell among them there are many, many who destroy their beard with a razor - since permission has been given to the destroyer [i.e., the razor], they do not distinguish between a razor and scissors or a depilatory. And many such evils follow from the freedom and evil customs, such as theaters and circuses and closeness in matters of forbidden relations, hand to hand - such a person shall not go unpunished. Not so in the kingdom of Ishmael, where the banner of Torah is raised high, they encamp and journey according to the Torah, and there is power and might in the hands of the sages and the leaders of the communities to break the jaws of the wicked and establish the faith on its foundation - and they [the gentiles there] are disciplined regarding forbidden relations, and are properly careful about [immodest] hearing, and a grown beard is esteemed among them. Although there is somewhat of an exile there too - a gentile man may strike a Hebrew man with a stone or a fist, and they burden them with taxes and levies, and devour Israel with a full mouth through wicked accusations, and sometimes the officers of the land strike and beat unlawfully and imprison them and leave them as prisoners of poverty and iron and frighten them with great fear, and many such evils - nevertheless, exile is fitting for Israel, for through this they are afflicted and crushed and raise their eyes upward and subject their hearts to their Father in Heaven, in the manner of Israel, who are likened to a doe, as stated in the Midrash (Bava Batra 16b): just as a doe cannot give birth until a snake comes and bites her womb, so Israel does not return in repentance except through a harsh king.
Pele Yoetz 47:7: And they have already said (Shemot Rabbah 21:5): "and Pharaoh drew near" (Exodus 14:10) - meaning that he drew Israel near to their Father in Heaven. And they said (Megillah 14a): great was the removal of the ring that Ahasuerus removed and gave to Haman, more than forty-eight prophets and seven prophetesses [who prophesied but did not effect as much repentance]. And so it shall be in the end of days - if Israel does not return in repentance, the Holy One, blessed be He, raises up against them a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman's, and turns them back to the good, and immediately they are redeemed. And moreover, according to the exile and the subjugation, so is the clarification of the sparks of holiness - as it is written (Exodus 1:12), "and just as they afflicted it, so it increased and so it spread." And this is what the Kabbalists explained regarding the verse (Ecclesiastes 8:9), "a time when man ruled over man to his own harm" - meaning that when a man of the husks rules over a man of holiness, it is to his own harm [i.e., the husk's], for he [the man of holiness] thereby clarifies the sparks of holiness from it. Behold, therefore, this is what the Merciful One said: either your annulment or the annulment of the son of Ishmael (Gittin 17a) - under Ishmael and not under Edom.
Pele Yoetz 47:8: And it is true that the man who fears the LORD from his youth shall find help against himself to serve God even in the cities of Edom, for there is a time for every desire, and nothing hinders him, and whoever wishes to serve the LORD can serve Him in any place and be guarded from all evil - and there it is recognizable that one who serves Him does so out of love. Nevertheless, it is fitting for a person not to establish his dwelling there; on the contrary, it is fitting to strive, if he can, to uproot his dwelling from there - for even though a person may know of himself that he fears the LORD and turns away from evil, who can guarantee that his own offspring shall be like him, and if, God forbid, in future generations some of his seed goes astray, the blood of his descendants hangs upon him. And at the very least, let him uproot his seed to the cities of Turkey before they take root in a root that bears gall and wormwood - for this too is a sick evil found in the cities of Edom, that they teach their children external wisdoms, the wisdom of philosophy, whose followers become heretics and unbelievers, of whom it is said (Proverbs 2:19), "none who go to her return, nor do they attain the paths of life." And it is true that our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sotah 47a): the favor of a place is upon its inhabitants, and all is the wonder of the One perfect in knowledge, who has scattered and placed each and every Israelite in the place where he is encamped - but nevertheless, the man whose eyes have been opened and who has taken to heart to choose a place fit for settlement, and who has the ability to uproot his dwelling, should flee and choose the best place for himself and his offspring for the service of God, blessed be He.
Pele Yoetz 47:9: And it is fitting for us, even in a place where there is freedom that lightens the burden of subjugation, to recognize in ourselves that we are captives, grieving and downtrodden, and our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, and slaves rule over us - and not to go about in grand and wondrous finery of garments and magnificent buildings, and not to increase in celebrations and rejoicing, and not to raise a voice of song with drums and dances. And even one whose boundary the LORD has widened should not show himself before the gentile nations of the lands, for the jealousy of the nations of the world toward Israel is as harsh as Sheol, and the little they see, their eyes shall darken from seeing and it shall seem to them like much - therefore men and women should be modest and not show their wealth and jewelry before gentiles, and when building houses they should build the exterior in a manner that it appears like a hut in a vineyard [i.e. modest]. And likewise it is fitting to be careful even from [the sight of] fellow Jews regarding the impression given, and to be very concerned about the great harm of the evil eye, and all the more so before gentiles. And it is known how much wandering and expulsion and many evils have passed over our souls because of the jealousy of the gentiles, since people were not careful not to show themselves - as brought regarding [the historical figure] Abarbanel, that he was so named because his wife had such a fine ring that everyone who saw her said "bravo, Anilya," and this caused the expulsion from Spain. And Jacob our father said to his sons: "why do you show yourselves?" (Genesis 42:1). And it is fitting for us to bend our heads like a reed and accept the exile with love, and to be mourners over the breaking of Joseph, that even if the peace of our table is full of richness, "woe to the children who are exiled from their father's table" - and how shall we sing on foreign soil? And it is written (Hosea 9:1): "do not rejoice, O Israel, with exultation like the nations." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 31a) that it is forbidden for a person to fill his mouth with laughter in this world, for it is said (Psalms 126:2), "then our mouths shall be filled with laughter and our tongues with joyous song; then shall they say among the nations, the LORD has done great things for these" - but now it is fitting for us to be grieving, brokenhearted, and downtrodden as we remember Zion and the many evils we have caused and the abundant good we have lost, and it is fitting that we set Jerusalem above the head of our joy and humble ourselves greatly - and through this God shall take counsel for us and hasten our redemption and build the Temple speedily in our days, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 48:1: Transmigration - Belief in the transmigration of souls awakens a person who wishes to take to heart the fear of the LORD, the fear of punishment - for he shall take to heart that among the many pains of the wicked, more bitter than death and than all the pangs of Gehinnom, is the evil of transmigration, that his soul be transmigrated into the mineral, vegetable, animal, and speaking [levels], and from evil to evil he goes out through transmigrations into different kinds of species, as explained in the books of the Kabbalists - and even for transgressions that seem light and that many have trampled upon, such as one who speaks slander [lashon hara], who is transmigrated into a barking dog - and your mnemonic sign is "and he called it [lah] Novach" (Numbers 32:42) - "lah" are the initial letters of "lashon hara." And one who gazes at forbidden women comes back in the transmigration of a bird called "Ra'ah" [a bird of prey], which "sins" through sight, and a sign for the matter: "and you shall not go about after your own heart and after your own eyes, after which you go astray" (ibid. 15:39). And the master Ari, of blessed memory, once saw the soul of a certain pious man who had been transmigrated into Boaz, because he had marital relations by candlelight and caused compulsion to his children. And there are many such kinds of transmigrations, as explained in the books of the Kabbalists. Let a man's hair stand on end and let him swiftly find an escape for himself while he is still alive, before the sun grows dark and his own regret shall be of no avail - for then his soul shall tremble and cry out in its pains, for it is bitter for the soul to be transmigrated into the mineral and vegetable, and into animals and beasts and birds and fish, both pure and impure, and every creeping thing of the earth - and even though when he is transmigrated as a human being he does not remember the previous transmigration, when he is in the mineral, vegetable, or animal state he remembers his beginning, that he was a prince and a great one, and his end was that he became a base fool, and his soul mourns over him. And it is already written in the books, and we too have heard with our own ears, awesome incidents from various transmigrations that were given permission to reveal themselves to the ear of the living in a dream, and especially to our teacher, the master Ari, of blessed memory, who saw visions of God, and saw thousands and myriads of souls who wept and pleaded with him to find rest for their souls. Of such matters, the living person shall take to heart and picture to himself as though it had happened to him, and shall swiftly find an escape for himself, while his hand can still attain redemption for himself.
Pele Yoetz 48:2: And also from among the beliefs of transmigration, one must be concerned that perhaps in a past transmigration he committed much impurity and guilt, and it is incumbent upon him to correct what he has perverted - and therefore let him go to great lengths to perform mitzvot and good deeds and mortifications and fasts and repairs, and even if the whole world tells him "you are righteous" and he himself knows that his deeds are pure and upright, let him be in his own eyes like a wicked man - as is known, their saying, of blessed memory (Niddah 30b), that this is what they say to a person at the time of his coming forth from his mother's womb, and one of the reasons for this is because of transmigration, for a person does not know what preceded him and what happened to him in the past transmigrations he underwent. And how much more so in these generations, since the Kabbalists have already revealed to us that most people are from past transmigrations, and it is rare to find a new soul that has come for the first time, and for this reason it is fitting that our hearts be humbled, for we have become very poor, and none of us knows what we are and what there is in us to repair, as it was in ancient days in the time of the master Ari, of blessed memory. Therefore it is fitting for a person to increase his good deeds, and let him always regard himself as a debtor, perhaps he shall find favor.
Pele Yoetz 48:3: And even though we do not know and do not recognize the previous transmigrations, one thing we know from the book of the Holy Zohar (Bereishit, page 92) - that whoever dies without children, God forbid, and his wife undergoes levirate marriage, the firstborn son she bears is himself the soul of the deceased who died childless, for his brother has become his father and his wife has become his mother - and it is fitting for the father and the acquaintances and friends of the deceased to tell him [the reincarnated child, when grown] the faults that were known to them, so that he can correct them as best he can.
Pele Yoetz 48:4: And also from belief in transmigration a person shall know that the judgments of the LORD are true - "the Rock, His work is perfect, for all His ways are just" (Deuteronomy 32:4) - and shall not complain about His attributes, blessed be He, as is the custom of some ignorant people among the nation who, when severe afflictions come upon them, open their mouths toward Heaven and say: Master of the universe, what is my transgression and what is my sin - have my sins and transgressions overpowered the whole world? Why do You do so to Your servants? If only they were wise, they would understand that "the Rock, His work is perfect, and all His ways are just" - "a God of faith without iniquity, just and upright is He" (ibid.), giving each man according to his ways and the fruit of his deeds, and to Him actions are measured. And if in this transmigration his deeds are pure and upright, these afflictions are for him because of past transmigrations - as is known, the saying of the Kabbalists, who revealed that the sufferings of Job, while he was blameless and upright and feared God and turned away from evil, were incurred because of a past transmigration, that he had been Terach, the father of Abraham our father, peace be upon him. And in this too there is reason to consider the severe sufferings that small children, weaned from the breast, endure, and the death of little ones - that for the sins of youth, the Holy One, blessed be He, sends into a man's wife a soul that owes a death penalty, to correct what it had perverted, and incidentally the father and mother find their own redemption through the distress they suffer at his death. And also through transmigrations are transmigrated the matters of matches, deaths, and all incidents - all of it is the wonder of the One perfect in knowledge, by measure, by weight, and by measure of capacity, as one who looks in the books of the Kabbalists that recount matters of transmigrations shall see with his own eyes and his heart shall understand and say: how great are Your works, O LORD, and how wondrous is His love for us, that He devised plans so that none banished from Him remain banished. Blessed be the Name of the LORD, blessed and exalted above all blessing and praise.
Pele Yoetz 49:1: Stranger - It is written (I Chronicles 29:15): "we are strangers on the earth," and it is written (Psalms 39:13), "for I am a stranger with You." And this is a great principle in all of Judaism: that a person should not go after excesses, and should not be exacting about foods, nor about clothing, nor about a fine dwelling, but rather, like a guest who turns aside to lodge on the road, so shall he be content with whatever comes to his hand, and his whole aim shall be toward the World to Come, for that is his home. And even whatever he pursues of matters of this world, his aim shall be to have preparation for himself to attain the paths of life, and let all his deeds be for the sake of Heaven (Avot 2:12), and let him not add beyond what is truly necessary for the needs of Heaven. And let not his inclination mislead him with vain and misleading claims, even though such is the way of the evil inclination, showing all excesses as though they were absolute necessities for the service of God, blessed be He - but extra understanding is needed to distinguish between the necessary and the excessive, and not to follow the counsel of his own inclination until its opponent, the good inclination, comes and examines it.
Pele Yoetz 49:2: And it is true that the halachic authorities wrote (Yoreh De'ah 159:1) regarding the ruling that it is forbidden to lend to a gentile with interest except for one's livelihood - that nowadays everything counts as for one's livelihood, since taxes, levies, and gifts and other expenses have multiplied - but I say that in the way a person wishes to go, they lead him (Makkot 10b). Whoever makes his occupation permanent and labors to grow rich through schemes and thinks his rooms shall be filled, the Holy One, blessed be He, arranges for him expenses that force him to spend much, and then he thinks: I did well to labor with my ten fingers to earn much, for otherwise from where would I have paid these expenses? And those of confused spirit do not know that if he had earned little, the Holy One, blessed be He, would also have arranged that his expenses be little. And if a person wishes to make his Torah study permanent, most of the day, and his occupation occasional, he is assured that he shall not lack his bread, sufficient for whatever he needs - for He has already promised that He gives bread to all flesh, for His kindness endures forever. And it is written (Psalms 145:16): "You open Your hand and satisfy the desire of every living thing." And whatever trouble, distress, and toil a person endures, to the point that sometimes he is troubled out of this world and the World to Come, all of it is because he wishes to pursue excesses and human pleasures - these are truly the afflictions of mankind, and this is the entire evil of man: he enjoys the fruits in this world - toil and anger, rising early and staying up late, eating the bread of sorrows (ibid. 127:2) - while the principal is kept for the World to Come, since the currency of this world is worthless, and they have eaten up their allotted portion because of sins, transgressions, and the neglect of Torah and mitzvot, and the like.
Pele Yoetz 49:3: And our first father, Jacob, the chosen one among the patriarchs, asked of the LORD only bread to eat and clothing to wear, and the Tanna already said (Avot 6:4): such is the way of Torah - you shall eat bread with salt, drink water in small measure, sleep on the ground, live a life of hardship, and labor in Torah. And it is true that in these generations one cannot rebuke his fellow about this and say to him, "see the words of the Tanna, who said bread with salt, not bread with meat," and the like, and said "water" not "wine," and "on the ground" not on fine pillows and cushions and the like - for if a person says to his fellow, "remove the splinter from between your teeth," his fellow shall answer him, "and remove the beam from between your own eyes." And moreover, we have an answer, that the Tanna was of a family of the healthy, but now we cannot eat bread with salt alone, only a slice of the Hamotzi bread [i.e., we need more sustenance], and therefore we need other pleasures, for "not by bread alone does man live." And this is true according to what we have become accustomed to, it has become for us a necessity, in the manner they said (Ketubot 67b): "sufficient for whatever he needs" (Deuteronomy 15:8) - even a horse to ride upon and a servant to run before him. But the Holy One, blessed be He, gives this to a person only according to his deeds - if he is meritorious, He gives him his food at its proper time, each according to how the Holy One, blessed be He, provides it for him, whether it be that he earns enough for his need or from charity, as in the incident brought in the Talmud (ibid.) of that poor man who was accustomed to dine on a fattened chicken and old wine - see there. But if he has no merit for this, he shall find many evils and troubles, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 114a): whoever eats fat [beyond his means] hides in the attic [from creditors]; whoever eats bitter herbs [i.e. lives frugally] lies down in the town square [with peace of mind]. And they said (ibid.): eat an onion and sit in the shade, and do not eat delicacies while your heart pursues you [with debt].
Pele Yoetz 49:4: And it is within a person's power to accustom his nature little by little to be content with little and be self-restrained, and it shall be good for him - and if he suffers because of it, such is our obligation and it is fitting for us to live a life of hardship for the sake of the Torah and the service of God, and for the destruction of the Temple and the neglect of Torah and service, and for the many evils we have caused through our sins - and therefore, even if the LORD has widened his boundary, let him always be self-restrained, and it shall be good for him. Go forth and learn from our holy fathers, who all their days were strangers upon the earth and did not turn to human pleasures, but rather were always dwellers in tents without any [permanent] house, and easily wandered from place to place. And when Jacob sought to dwell in tranquility, immediately the trouble of Joseph sprang upon him (Rashi, Vayeshev 37:2). All the more so we, orphans of orphans, full of iniquities - if we seek pleasures, we shall consume our [share in the] World [to Come] in our own lifetimes, God forbid, and what shall we eat in the World to Come? And it is true that they said (Eruvin 54a), "if you have, do good for yourself" - this means not to reduce below what is necessary, according to what kind of person he is, the place, and the time - then, if he has the means, he may spend according to his needs; but if he does not have it, it is not fitting for him to labor to grow rich in order to make large expenditures, and it is better that he earn little and spend little, like a wayfarer passing through, and not multiply toil to become like Korah, for this causes him to become impoverished from both sides. But whoever is like a stranger in this world shall build for himself a faithful house for the World to Come, for he shall be beloved on high - for in thirty-six places the Torah commanded love of the stranger, and the Holy One, blessed be He, as it were, is the first to fulfill the entire Torah, and He loves the stranger, giving him bread and clothing - and it is within every person's power to make himself a stranger in the land, insofar as he humbles himself like the soul of a stranger and does not seek to pursue grand and wondrous things.
Pele Yoetz 49:5: And since the Torah commanded so much regarding love of the stranger, if it happens that a righteous convert comes, it is fitting to have very great mercy on him, and to grant him gifts of money, and to seek for him a resting place that shall be good for him, and to appease him with good words - even though it is highly suspected that he shall return to his former evil ways, as our eyes see - nevertheless, because of this, the one who does good for him should not regret his previous good deed, God forbid, and should not withdraw his hand from doing good to other converts, for we have nothing but to see him as he is now and fulfill our Maker's commandment - and if afterward he goes astray into bad ways, he alone has caused loss to his own soul, while the reward for the mitzvah stands forever.
Pele Yoetz 49:6: And included in the mitzvah of love of converts is to help and assist a man wandering from his own place who is a stranger in a foreign land - and not necessarily a righteous convert, for is it a case of "one who is established in the land, and a stranger in the highest heavens" [i.e. it applies broadly]? Rather, follow the reasoning, as it is written (Exodus 23:9): "and you know the soul of the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt." Behold, the verse speaks explicitly of one who is a stranger in a foreign land, without friend or brother, with no one who knows him, his spirit low and his heart broken and crushed - it is fitting to have mercy on him and draw him near and be to him a friend and companion, and to help and support him with whatever comes to hand, and thereby he fulfills this great mitzvah.
Pele Yoetz 49:7: And this mitzvah is all the greater regarding an Ashkenazi walking among Sephardim, or a Sephardi among Ashkenazim, and the like - for they do not even share a language, so that one does not hear the language of his fellow, and they are greatly downtrodden, unable to express their distress or show their own worth - for there are among them masters of Torah too, but they have no mouth to speak, and a mask of shame is upon their faces, and they have no forehead to lift their head. Toward these it is especially fitting to have mercy, and it shall be counted a great mitzvah - not as many of the common people say, that a Sephardi should go to Sephardim and an Ashkenazi to Ashkenazim, and each kind should have mercy on its own kind, as though we were two separate nations, God forbid - certainly whoever says this has blasphemed the ranks of the living God, for it is a disgrace to us, the children of Israel, one nation in the land, that a man should separate himself from his brothers, since we are all sons of one man, one God for all of us, one Father for all of us, one Torah and one law - why should we betray one another? And if the languages differ by land, what does that matter, and what difference is there between a Sephardi and an Ashkenazi or other languages - heaven forbid to make any distinction; on the contrary, the obligation to have mercy on and assist one who speaks a different language should be all the greater, by reason of the mitzvah of love of the stranger, as stated. And whoever has mercy is shown mercy from Heaven, and the LORD shall repay the one who does good sevenfold.
Pele Yoetz 50:1: Great - Great is our Master, and of His greatness there is no fathoming, beyond a place our own hand can reach. And it is already written in Sefer HaCharedim that just as a small child who can count only up to ten, when told "beyond fathoming and beyond number," it comes into his mind to picture that a hundred is beyond fathoming and beyond number, and when he learns to count to a hundred, it comes into his mind to picture that a thousand or ten thousand is beyond fathoming and beyond number - so too, whatever we confine within our own understanding of the greatness of our Master, we cannot manage to picture even to the degree of a small child who can count only to ten. And in any case, it is fitting for us to remember always, as much as we can, the greatness of our Master, to a place our own hand can reach, upon seeing the greatness of this lowly world - and it is as nothing compared to what is higher than it, and higher still above that, and above them are troops upon troops and myriads upon myriads beyond fathoming and beyond number - and all of it is as nothing compared to the greatness of our Master. And let us believe with complete faith that our own hand cannot reach to understand and picture the greatness of our Master, one part in a thousand thousands of thousands and myriads of myriads, and we are not permitted to reckon Him at all, as it is written in the opening of [the prayer attributed to] Elijah: "no thought can grasp You at all." And so said the Psalmist: "of the fathoming of His works" - "but to Him do not send your hand" [i.e. do not presume to fathom Him]. And this thought is beneficial when combined with reckoning, against it, the lowliness of man and the abundant goodness and love of the Creator toward him - it arouses love and fear and humility and joy, and from this is drawn all unification [of God's Name] and pure fear of the LORD. Happy is the man who persists in this thought from time to time, for it is itself a mitzvah, and draws another mitzvah, and guards against every debt, and makes his service a complete service. And this was the practice of the early pious ones, who would tarry one hour before every prayer (Berachot 30b) to reckon the greatness of the Creator and the lowliness of man, and afterward stand to pray as befits a gnat standing to serve before a high and exalted King, awesome and fearsome. This is a great principle in the Torah, and this applies to every person.
Pele Yoetz 50:2: And behold, the Holy One, blessed be He - His is the greatness and His is the fitting honor, and He has shared a portion of His own honor with His creatures and commanded that each one give honor to whoever is greater than himself - such as to father and mother, to a teacher, and to whoever is greater than himself in wisdom or in years - and likewise a brother is obligated to honor his brother who is older than himself, and similarly, whoever is greater than his fellow, his fellow is obligated to honor him - for so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 113b): from where do we know that when one recognizes in his fellow that he is greater than himself, he is obligated to treat him with honor? As it is said (Daniel 6:4), "for an extraordinary spirit was found in him." And whoever disgraces one to whom he is obligated in honor is as though he disgraces the Holy One, blessed be He, who commanded regarding his honor.
